title: The Illusory Truth Effect
description: Repetition, not evidence, makes a claim feel true.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Hearing something repeatedly makes it feel truer, even when you were told at the start that it was false. Familiarity is quietly mistaken for accuracy.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The brain uses ease of processing as a cue for truth. A statement you have seen before is read more fluently, and that fluency feels like recognition — a signal that it must be right.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: A rumour repeated across enough headlines begins to sound like established fact.
Advertising slogans you can recite often feel more credible than products you have actually researched.
A false claim repeated in meetings over weeks is eventually treated as background truth.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: A claim that keeps returning with no new evidence behind it.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Repetition is fair when the underlying claim is true and sourced. Consistent messaging helps accurate ideas stick.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Repeating a false or unverified claim until familiarity does the work that evidence cannot.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: You believe something but cannot recall where you first heard it.
The only support for a claim is how often you have heard it.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: When a claim feels obviously true, ask: what is the actual evidence?
Trace claims to a source before accepting them.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Assuming that knowing a claim is false protects you from the effect. It does not.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: Repetition builds belief independently of truth.
Ask where you first learned it.
